Stage 2c: the refined linked core

Four refinements at zero cost in degrees of freedom — closing the monetary loop, and the fifth refinement that had to be thrown away

Summary

Stage 2c refines stage 2b’s eleven-country system. Its defining property is that the refinements are free: k stays at 76 against T = 98, so df = 22 in both systems. Every stage-3 block in this project bought structure with degrees of freedom — stage 3a went to df = 15, then 6; stage 3b to 8; stage 3c could not be validated at all. Stage 2c is the one extension that can be compared against its predecessor with no size caveat attached.

Five refinements were estimated. Four are adopted; one is rejected.

# Refinement Verdict
1 prices gains <iso2>_gdp (Phillips curve) Adopted. The monetary loop closes: ea_policy_rate goes from reaching no price variable at all to reaching every one. 10 of 11 correctly signed.
2 foreign_demand over partner imports Adopted. Largely a rescaling — partner imports are ~1.8x as volatile as partner GDP — though the US index genuinely changes.
3 Model the spread; long_rate becomes an identity Adopted. Motivation confirmed emphatically: all eleven stage-2b policy-rate loadings straddle zero. One stated benefit is not delivered.
4 consumption gains <iso2>_long_rate Adopted, weak. 8 of 11 correctly signed, and the loadings are small.
5 imports gains <iso2>_exports (import content) Rejected. Collapses the domestic-demand elasticity in 9 of 11 countries while halving the imports equations’ RMSE.

The recommended system is clean on every sampler diagnostic: 0 acceptance-rate flags of 68, 0 lag-stability flags, and 8 sign-check failures of 55.

The most useful thing this stage produced is the rejection. Refinement 5 improves in-sample fit dramatically and breaks the model, and it took three separate diagnostics — an elasticity comparison, a re-estimation without it, and a sign-check count corrected for absent terms — to see that. Section 4 is the substance of this report.

1. Four refinements, none of which costs a degree of freedom

All three systems are the same size. Only the identity count moves.
system stochastic identities endogenous exogenous k T_obs df seconds
stage 2b 68 35 103 7 76 98 22 213.5
stage 2c (recommended, 4 refinements) 68 46 114 7 76 98 22 287.7
stage 2c + import content (rejected) 68 46 114 7 76 98 22 294.1

The equation count is unchanged at 68 stochastic, because the long-rate level equation is swapped for a spread equation rather than added to. Identities go 35 → 46: eleven new <iso2>_long_rate == 1*<iso2>_spread + 1*<policy rate>.

Why each refinement is free:

  • 1 and 4 add only contemporaneous endogenous regressors. k = 1 + (one lag per stochastic equation) + (exogenous), and a contemporaneous endogenous term is none of those three.
  • 2 re-weights an existing identity; the weights are fixed trade shares.
  • 3 is k-neutral by construction: the long rate loses its own lag column and the spread gains one.

The second k constraint is slack too. draw_omega_j() draws riwish(T - k, .) on a matrix that is (endogenous regressors in that equation + 1) square, so the binding requirement here is df >= 3 against df = 22.

1.1 A silent identity violation, found and closed off

Stage 2c is the first configuration to put the US in spread_countries, and that exposed a live trap. <iso2>_long_rate == <iso2>_spread + <policy rate> is written in two places that must agree: the identity, and the <iso2>_spread series the panel builder constructs. The identity resolved us_policy_rate for the US under policy_rule = TRUE; the panel builder’s scalar default subtracted ea_policy_rate for everyone. The US identity was violated by the entire EA–US policy-rate gap — up to 3.25 percentage points — and koma said nothing, because koma has no identity-consistency check at all.

Both sides now resolve through one policy_rate_map(), and stage2_preflight() gained a ninth check, identity_consistency(), which does the arithmetic koma does not: it recomputes every identity from the panel and reports its worst absolute error, in level space for the rate/none rate family and in rate space for everything else. On the stage-2c panel, 23 exact identities hold to a worst error of 1.05e-13. <iso2>_gdp and <iso2>_domestic_demand are reported but never flagged — the first holds only up to the statistical discrepancy, the second is deliberately inexact under include_government = FALSE.

2. The loop that was open

CLAUDE.md has recorded since stage 1 that “making a variable endogenous does not give it a transmission channel”. Stage 2b gave ea_policy_rate its own Taylor rule; reports/stage2_spillovers.qmd §4 then found no monetary transmission at all, and §7.2 recorded the sanity check failing as a genuine property of the fitted system rather than a code defect.

contemporaneous_reachability() says exactly where the break was.

Endogenous variables reachable from ea_policy_rate through contemporaneous links.
system endogenous reached price_variables_reached
stage 2b 103 91 0
stage 2c (recommended) 114 114 12

Stage 2b’s policy rate reaches 91 of 103 endogenous variables — and not one of them is a price. It is even reachable from itself, through the Taylor rule’s ea_gdp term, so a naive “is the loop closed?” test would have passed. The rule’s output term was closed all along; its inflation term was the open one, responding to a variable nothing the rule did could influence.

The price equation was the break. In stage 2b its contemporaneous endogenous regressor set was empty — own lag, COVID dummies, eur_usd and oil_price, all exogenous. Adding <iso2>_gdp closes it, and stage 2c’s policy rate reaches all 114 endogenous variables, all 12 price variables included.

There is a second, mechanical confirmation. An equation with no contemporaneous endogenous regressor gets no Metropolis step, so koma reports count_accepted = NA for it:

The eleven stage-2b equations with no Metropolis step were exactly the price equations.
system with_metropolis_step without which_without
stage 2b 57 11 at_prices, be_prices, de_prices, gr_prices, es_prices, fr_prices, ie_prices, it_prices, nl_prices, pt_prices, us_prices
stage 2c 68 0 —

Structure is not magnitude. Reachability says a path exists, not that anything travels along it — §4.5 and §8 put numbers on that.

3. Estimation and the sampler

Equations outside the 20-60% acceptance band at each tune_tau_system() round.
system iteration 0 iteration 1 iteration 2 iteration 3
stage 2c + import content 14 6 1 0
stage 2c (recommended) 23 6 0 NA

Both configurations converge, the recommended one in two rounds. Two things about that table are worth stating rather than glossing.

First, the five-refinement run’s iteration 0 flags 14 where a separately estimated untuned fit of the same system flagged 9. That is not a change: model_identification() consumes RNG, so two estimations of the same system give slightly different acceptance rates, and a dozen equations sit within a percentage point of the 60% boundary. Reading 9 → 14 as a finding would be reading noise.

Second, the tuned recommended system has 0 equations outside the band and 0 lag-stability flags. The sampler is not the explanation for anything in what follows.

4. Refinement 5, and why it had to go

This is the substance of the report, so it is worth stating the shape of the argument before the tables. The import-content term — giving <iso2>_imports a contemporaneous <iso2>_exports regressor, on the sound reasoning that exports require imported intermediates — passes its own sign check in 11 of 11 countries and improves the imports equations’ in-sample fit dramatically. It is still wrong, and three separate diagnostics were needed to establish that.

4.1 The sign check saw one failure; nine elasticities were being gutted

imports ~ domestic_demand. The elasticity the equation exists to measure.
equation stage 2b with import content recommended
at_imports 0.450 -0.104 0.274
be_imports 0.849 0.621 0.832
de_imports 0.382 0.049 0.320
es_imports 1.705 1.569 1.742
fr_imports 1.245 0.638 1.215
gr_imports 1.000 0.833 0.862
ie_imports 0.650 0.699 0.663
it_imports 1.213 0.803 1.278
nl_imports 1.027 1.126 1.013
pt_imports 1.491 1.306 1.503
us_imports 1.798 1.237 1.782

With the term in, nine of eleven elasticities fall and two are destroyed: Germany from 0.382 to 0.049, Austria from 0.450 to −0.104. Only Austria crosses zero, so sign_checks() — which looks at one coefficient at a time — reported exactly one failure while most of the block was being hollowed out.

CLAUDE.md already contains this lesson in the abstract (“a wrong sign is often not the first symptom — a neighbouring coefficient moving is”) and this failure in the concrete: four attempts at putting an import price into this same equation, of which the contemporaneous one “collapses the domestic-demand elasticity from 0.38 to 0.08”. Substituting exports for import_prices lands German demand elasticity at 0.049 — the same number, by the same mechanism. Exports and imports share the trade cycle, so a contemporaneous export term is an excellent predictor of imports and a direct competitor to domestic demand for the same variance.

4.2 The improved fit is the symptom, not the reassurance

In-sample RMSE of the imports equations. Ratio below 1 is a better fit.
equation stage 2b RMSE with import content ratio
be_imports 1.8145 0.6471 0.3566
nl_imports 1.8202 0.9271 0.5093
es_imports 1.9303 1.0135 0.5251
ie_imports 4.7966 3.4560 0.7205
fr_imports 1.5103 1.1269 0.7461
at_imports 2.1432 1.6590 0.7741
it_imports 1.7637 1.3790 0.7819
de_imports 1.9917 1.5780 0.7923
us_imports 1.3460 1.1092 0.8241

Belgium’s imports equation fits 2.8x better and the Netherlands’ 2.0x better, while their structural elasticities fall. That is what a contemporaneous regressor correlated with the dependent variable does, whether or not it belongs there. Had this stage been judged on in-sample fit — the five-refinement system fits better in 77% of shared equations — the term would have been adopted.

4.3 Removing it recovers every elasticity, and repairs equations it never touched

Sign-check failures. Both columns are over the same 55 checks.
check with_import_content recommended
import_elasticity_positive 1 0
phillips_curve_positive 3 1
consumption_rate_channel_negative 5 3
spread_loads_on_prices_positive 3 3
mpc_in_0_1 0 1
TOTAL (of 55 comparable checks) 12 8

All eleven elasticities move back toward their stage-2b values (Germany 0.320 against 0.382, France 1.215 against 1.245, the US 1.782 against 1.798) — the same recovery stage 3a saw when the import-price term was lagged, “0.386 vs 0.382”.

The wider effect is the interesting one. Removing a term from the imports equation repairs two Phillips-curve sign checks and two consumption-rate sign checks, in equations it does not appear in. In a simultaneous system with a system-wide residual covariance, one badly specified equation is not a local problem — which is the other half of a lesson CLAUDE.md already carries from stage 3a phase B: “a bad specification in one equation can masquerade as a systemic problem”. Here it masqueraded as two.

The one thing that gets worse is Ireland’s MPC, which crosses from +0.001 to −0.005. Ireland’s consumption–GDP loading is ~0 in all three systems (0.017 in stage 2b), so this is a coefficient that is not identified rather than one that broke; it is reported here rather than explained away.

4.4 A reporting trap this exposed

Read naively, sign_checks(stage2c = TRUE) reports 19 failures of 66 for the recommended system against 12 of 66 for the rejected one — the opposite of the truth. Eleven of those nineteen are import_content_positive scoring NA/FALSE because the term is not in the model.

That default is right for the stage-3 blocks it was designed for (“a check that could not be evaluated is not a check that passed”) and wrong for a deliberately dropped refinement. sign_checks(stage2c = ) now takes a subset of stage2c_refinements(), and stage2c_config() returns the subset it carries.

iso2 median q05 q95 share_ge_1 consumption_long_rate phillips taylor
at 0 -0.0002 0.0002 0 0.0315 0.0670 0.2571
be 0 -0.0005 0.0003 0 -0.0065 0.1233 0.2571
de 0 -0.0013 0.0017 0 -0.0985 -0.0383 0.2571
gr 0 -0.0001 0.0001 0 -0.1170 0.0017 0.2571
es 0 -0.0010 0.0011 0 -0.0059 0.2138 0.2571
fr 0 -0.0008 0.0008 0 0.0306 0.0725 0.2571
ie 0 -0.0001 0.0000 0 -0.1240 0.0134 0.2571
it 0 -0.0013 0.0010 0 -0.0001 0.0500 0.2571
nl 0 -0.0006 0.0004 0 -0.0018 0.0065 0.2571

No draw in any country reaches a round-trip gain of 1, so the loop stage 2c adds is not a stability risk. CLAUDE.md warns against reading that as reassurance — “a quiet loop is not necessarily a stable one” — so the per-link means are in the table, and they are the point:

  • The Taylor rule’s inflation loading is 0.257, positive and sensible, shared by every country.
  • The Phillips curve link is positive in 9 of the 10 euro-area countries, up to 0.214. Germany is the exception, at -0.038.
  • The consumption rate channel is the weak link: correctly signed in most countries but tiny, and positive in Austria and France.

A six-link chain of coefficients this small multiplies out to a contemporaneous gain around 1e-5. That is a statement about within-quarter feedback, not about whether a monetary shock has any effect over a horizon — the dynamic response accumulates through the lag structure, which is what §8 measures.

5. The rate block: from a level equation to a spread equation

The stage-2b long-rate equation against the stage-2c spread equation.
iso2 long_rate_own_lag_2b policy_loading_2b spans_zero_2b spread_own_lag_2c
at 0.937 0.046 TRUE 0.936
be 0.942 0.041 TRUE 0.958
de 0.940 0.045 TRUE 0.933
es 0.961 0.005 TRUE 0.983
fr 0.915 0.052 TRUE 0.935
gr 0.945 -0.049 TRUE 0.958
ie 0.962 0.007 TRUE 0.968
it 0.910 0.031 TRUE 0.957
nl 0.917 0.064 TRUE 0.937
pt 0.964 -0.013 TRUE 0.979
us 0.926 0.015 TRUE 0.937

The motivation for refinement 3 is confirmed, and more strongly than the design note claimed. All eleven stage-2b policy-rate loadings have 90% credible intervals straddling zero, while the long rate’s own lag sits at 0.910–0.964. The level equation was an AR(1) with decoration, and imposing the pass-through at 1 is strictly better than estimating it into insignificance.

One of the four stated benefits does not survive contact with the data. The design note argued that “a spread is stationary where a rate level is not, so the own lag has no unit root to run to”. The stage-2c spread own lags run 0.933–0.983 — as persistent as the levels they replaced, and for Spain (0.961 → 0.983) and Portugal (0.964 → 0.979) more so. The other three arguments are unaffected. The roxygen for financial_block() has been corrected to say so.

7. In-sample fit

Against stage 2b. Both systems estimated on the identical 2000Q1-2024Q4 window.

Read the two columns together and the case against refinement 5 completes itself. The rejected system’s headline is better on every summary line — until the imports equations are separated out, at which point its entire advantage is there and nowhere else: every other equation’s median ratio is ~1.000.

The recommended system’s improvement is the opposite shape: small, and spread across the equations that are not imports (median ratio 0.9983 against 1.0001 for imports, which is unchanged because nothing in refinement 1–4 touches that equation). That is what a genuine structural improvement looks like: modest, diffuse, and not concentrated in the equation that gained a regressor.

8. The monetary shock, re-run

The whole point of refinement 1 was reports/stage2_spillovers.qmd §4: a +100bp/4-quarter ea_policy_rate shock produced “no evidence of a real transmission channel” on the stage-2b system, and §7.2 recorded the sanity check failing as a genuine property of the fitted linkage. Stage 2c closes the structural gap. This section asks whether that changed the numbers.

The battery is run exactly as stage 2b’s was — same 8-quarter horizon, same shock definitions, same scenario_diff() common-random-numbers pairing.

8.1 The failing draws, recovered rather than worked around

The sustained 4-quarter restriction makes koma’s conditional solve singular for 40 of 1000 draws: restricting four horizons at once requires inverting R %*% Omega %*% t(R), and for a numerically rank-deficient draw no valid conditional innovation exists. koma drops those by subsetting the list, so scenario_diff() aborts on the draw-count mismatch rather than silently mispair the two legs.

failed_restriction_draws() re-derives the indices by tracing koma:::forecast_draw() and asking, per draw, whether it returned normally. Two verifications before using them:

  • The verification stage 2b applied holds here too: all 40 are also flagged explosive in the unconditional baseline (549 of 1000 draws exceed |de_gdp| > 100 at horizon 8). The same badly-behaved population surfaces as an outright failure under a demanding restriction and as a blow-up without one — not a new failure mode.
  • The failing set is identical at both seeds — the same 40 indices, not merely the same count. That is the prediction the mechanism makes (failure depends on the draw’s posterior Omega, which carries no RNG; the innovation draw is what the seed controls), and it holds on the production system rather than only on a test fixture.

Read on its own, this looks like progress: cumulative GDP moves from negative in 6 of 11 to 8 of 11, and Germany, Greece and Ireland now peak negative at horizons 4, 6 and 2 rather than showing a positive horizon-1 spike and nothing after. Greece’s path is the most transmission-shaped thing in the battery: −0.15, −0.18, −0.18, −0.23, −0.27, −0.18, −0.27 from horizon 2 on — persistent, negative, not decaying.

Most of that is the seed. CLAUDE.md requires a placebo before reporting any such change, and here it removes the headline outright.

The count of countries with a negative cumulative GDP response is 8 at seed A and 6 at seed B — and 6 in stage 2b. The stage-2c “improvement” is smaller than the distance between two runs of stage 2c itself, so it is not a finding.

Mean seed-to-seed gap 0.250 against a mean cross-system gap of 0.409 — the same order of magnitude. For 7 of the eleven the cross-system gap is smaller than the seed spread, and 2 cumulative responses flip sign between the two seeds.

What does survive is gr, ie, pt. Two of those are substantive: Greece’s cross-system gap is 1.78 against a seed spread of 0.19, and Ireland’s 1.05 against 0.32, both moving strongly more contractionary under stage 2c — and both are among the three countries whose response peaks at a later horizon. Portugal clears the same 2x bar only because its seed spread happens to be unusually small (0.030); its actual movement is 0.17pp and in the opposite direction, slightly less contractionary, so it is better read as a country the placebo cannot resolve than as a third finding. Germany’s gap (0.43) is not clearly above its seed spread (0.37) and should not be claimed at all.

What has not changed at all is the horizon-1 echo. Eight of eleven still peak at horizon 1 with a positive value, which §1.3 of the stage-2b report diagnosed as a same-quarter simultaneity artefact of imposing an exact-value restriction, not a transmission effect.

8.3 Prices: the loop is closed and the sign is wrong

Price response to the same shock.

at 1 0.0072 0.0177 1 0.0151 0.0221

Every one of the eleven price peaks is positive, in both systems — a monetary tightening appearing to raise prices. Stage 2c did not fix this; if anything it is marginally worse (1 negative peaks in stage 2b, 0 in stage 2c).

The mechanism is legible from §4.5’s per-link means, and it is not that the price block is broken. The Phillips-curve link is positive and correctly signed in 10 of 11 countries: prices rise when GDP rises. But the policy shock’s effect on GDP is positive at horizon 1 — the simultaneity echo — and the price response is almost entirely a horizon-1 effect that decays to zero rather than turning negative. Prices are faithfully tracking the wrong part of the GDP path.

The cost-push channel, by contrast, is correctly signed and substantial:

All eleven positive, cumulative 0.8–2.3pp. So the price equation responds sensibly to a genuine cost shock and perversely to a policy rate. That localises the remaining problem: it is not the price block, it is that the policy rate’s route into GDP is dominated by a within-quarter artefact rather than by a lagged demand channel.

The three spillover sanity checks, both systems.
check stage2b stage2c
own effect exceeds every cross-country effect FAIL — 7/11 countries: own > max|cross| PASS — 11/11 countries: own > max|cross|
monetary contraction is negative for GDP and prices everywhere FAIL — GDP peak negative: 2/11 | prices peak negative: 1/11 FAIL — GDP peak negative: 3/11 | prices peak negative: 0/11
spillover magnitude correlates with bilateral trade weight FAIL — Spearman rho = 0.141 (pass threshold: > 0.3) FAIL — Spearman rho = 0.292 (pass threshold: > 0.3)

One of the three checks goes from fail to pass, and it is the structural one. Stage 2b’s own-effect check failed for four countries: a French, German or Belgian demand shock moved Austrian GDP more than it moved the source’s own, an indirect two-hop path through Germany that §7.1 of that report analysed at length and concluded was a legitimate property of a simultaneous system rather than a defect. Under stage 2c the own effect dominates in 11 of 11, and the diagonals are far more uniform (0.955–1.553 against stage 2b’s 0.782–1.662).

The trade-weight correlation more than doubles, from ρ = 0.141 to ρ = 0.292, though it still misses the 0.3 threshold.

That number would not exist at all without a fix made for this stage. spillover_sanity_checks() looked each source up as <source>_gdp in the receiver’s foreign_demand weights. Stage 2c’s identity loads partner imports, so every lookup missed, the weight column came out all zeros, and the reported correlation was computed against a constant — a meaningless verdict rather than an error. The lookup now matches on the ISO-2 prefix, which also repairs the same latent bug under ireland_proxy.

9.1 Placebo: how much of this is the seed?

CLAUDE.md is emphatic that an individual spillover cell is not a reliable number at 1000 draws — re-running the same battery on the same fit with only the seed changed moves an off-diagonal cell by 0.35pp on average and flips the sign of 7–10 of 30. So before reading anything above as a stage-2c effect, the same four source countries were re-run at a second seed on the same fit.

Four source countries (de, fr, it, nl) x 11 receivers = 44 cells.
comparison mean_abs_diff max_abs_diff sign_flips
seed A vs seed B, same stage-2c fit (noise) 0.119 0.356 1
stage 2c vs stage 2b, same seed (the claim) 0.396 1.675 3

Unlike §8.2, the matrix survives its placebo. The cross-system difference (mean 0.396) is more than three times the seed-to-seed spread (0.119), and 26 of the 44 cells move by more than twice the noise.

There is a second, more interesting reading of that same table. CLAUDE.md records the stage-2b matrix’s own seed sensitivity: re-running it at a second seed moved an off-diagonal cell by 0.35pp on average, up to 1.85, and flipped the sign of 7–10 of 30. The equivalent numbers for stage 2c are 0.119, 0.356, and 1 of 44. The stage-2c spillover matrix is roughly three times more reproducible than stage 2b’s. That is not a claim that can itself be dismissed as noise — it is a measurement of the noise, and it is the strongest single result in this report.

Own diagonals: is the stage-2b-to-2c gap larger than the seed-to-seed spread?
country own_2b own_2c_seedA own_2c_seedB seed_spread system_gap
de 1.378 1.481 1.298 0.183 0.103
fr 1.658 1.448 1.432 0.016 0.210
it 1.371 1.163 1.129 0.034 0.209
nl 1.008 1.290 1.311 0.021 0.282

Cell by cell the diagonals behave as the placebo would demand: France, Italy and the Netherlands move by ~10x their seed spread and can be reported; Germany’s diagonal moves by less than its own seed spread (0.103 against 0.183) and must not be. That is the same discipline the stage-3c report applied, and it lands on a different country this time.

10. Verdict

Adopt stage 2c, with four refinements, not five. It is the first extension in this project that costs nothing: k = 76 and df = 22, identical to stage 2b, so nothing here trades structure against degrees of freedom. stage2c_config() and the _targets.R stage-2c chain build the recommended system.

What it demonstrably buys:

  1. A structurally closed monetary loop. ea_policy_rate reaches all 114 endogenous variables including all 12 prices, against 91 of 103 and zero prices in stage 2b. This is exact and verifiable, not estimated.
  2. A materially better spillover structure. The own-effect sanity check goes from 7/11 (fail) to 11/11 (pass); the stage-2b Austria artefact is gone; the trade-weight correlation more than doubles (0.141 → 0.292, still short of the 0.3 threshold).
  3. A three-times more reproducible spillover matrix — mean seed-to-seed movement 0.119 against stage 2b’s 0.35, and 1 sign flip in 44 cells against 7–10 in 30. For a battery whose individual cells CLAUDE.md warns should never be read one at a time, this is the most useful improvement of the three.
  4. A tidier rate block. All eleven stage-2b policy-rate loadings straddled zero; imposing the pass-through at 1 and modelling the spread removes eleven coefficients that were never identified.

What it does not buy, stated plainly:

  • A working monetary transmission. The price response to a +100bp tightening is positive at peak in all eleven countries — the wrong sign — and the GDP response still concentrates in a horizon-1 simultaneity echo. The apparent improvement in cumulative GDP sign (6/11 → 8/11) does not survive the seed placebo: the same fit gives 6/11 at a second seed. Only Greece and Ireland show a change larger than seed noise. Closing a loop structurally is necessary and, on this evidence, nowhere near sufficient.
  • A better in-sample fit. Median RMSE ratio 0.9992; the improvement is real but small and diffuse.
  • A stationary spread. Refinement 3’s persistence argument is contradicted by its own estimates (own lags 0.933–0.983 against 0.910–0.964).

And the most valuable thing the stage produced is a rejection. Refinement 5 — the import-content term — improves in-sample fit in the imports equations by up to 2.8x and passes its own sign check 11 of 11, while collapsing the domestic-demand elasticity in 9 of 11 countries and corrupting four sign checks in equations it never touches. Every diagnostic that looks at the term itself approves it. Only comparing it against the specification without it exposes it. That is the third time this project has met the same failure in the same equation, and the standing conclusion holds: the imports volume equation takes domestic demand and its own lag, and nothing contemporaneous.

Eight-quarter forecast

8 quarters from 2025Q1 to 2026Q4, 1000 posterior draws. Actuals exist for the first 5 quarters; the rest is genuinely ahead of the data.

Every fan below is the filtered predictive interval: koma constrains no draw to be stationary, so a draw whose quarterly growth exceeds 100% in absolute value is dropped before the quantiles are taken, exactly as score_forecast() does when it scores a backtest. The solid band is the 25th-75th percentile of what survives, the faint band the 10th-90th, the dark line their median, and the grey line the realised path where one exists. Across the variables shown, 1.8% of draws are discarded as explosive at horizon 1, rising to 48.0% at horizon 8 (worst: gr_gdp at 61.0%). A variable whose discarded share climbs steeply is one whose fan understates the model’s true uncertainty, so read the tail of a wide fan as an ordering rather than a number.

The panels are clipped, and that is worth saying plainly. Eight quarters out, the 10-90 interval on quarterly growth spans tens of percentage points in every stage of this project – an honest number, and one that makes the median invisible if the axis is scaled to contain it. Each panel is therefore scaled to its inner band, and the outer band runs to the panel edge rather than being drawn in full. Nothing is concealed: the table at the end of this section reports the untruncated bounds.

Every level path is anchored on an observed value (largest anchor discrepancy 0.00%, on at_imports), so the level and rate charts are both directly comparable to the actuals.

A forecast this long needs the exogenous series to reach the end of the horizon, and they do not: every one of them stops at the fit’s own native forecast end. extend_forecast_horizon() carries each one forward on its trailing four-quarter average growth – a momentum continuation, not a view on oil markets or world trade – and koma would otherwise have silently returned a shorter horizon than the one requested.
